- *The advanced source's spelling.* The quotes in this chapter keep their source's spelling, which writes lax vowels the newer orthography hears in more places: **awëx**, **q'ayïs**, **k'ïy**, **chïk**, **töq**, **niqatïk**, **wakamïn** where this book writes **awex**, **q'ayis**, **k'iy**, **chik**, **töq**/**toq**, **nqatik**, **wakami**. Same words, same speakers, twenty years of orthographic drift. Read both without blinking.
- *-jäch' means "harvest the ears".* Our main source's dictionary glosses it "harvest", and the advanced source's own chapter vocabulary agrees ("tapiscar"), though its glossary once says "shuck". Shucking, taking the husks off, is **-elesaj rij** or **-pöch'** (Chapter 24). Keep the two jobs apart.
- *chuw or chüw.* The 2006 dictionary writes **chüw** "stinky" with a lax vowel; the advanced source writes **chuw** and its verb **-chuwïr**. This book writes **chuw**.
- *k'ok' is two smells and a texture.* The dictionary says "smelling spicy" (toasting chiles); the advanced source's smell sidebar says "burnt smell or taste" and uses it for scorched food, and its kitchen list also has **k'ok' ke'en** "finely ground dough". All three are attested; context sorts them out.
- *q'or twice.* **q'or** "atole" and **q'or** "lazy" (Chapter 25) are homophones. **Nuqüm q'or ri q'or** would be "the lazy one drinks atole"; nobody will say it, but everyone will enjoy that you know it.
- *awän agreement.* **Awän** is grammatically a mass-like noun but takes plural agreement when the individual plants are in view: **yetzaq ri awän**, **e q'ochöl ri awän**. With the field as a place, singular: **nim ri awän** "the milpa is big".
- *tür, the smut.* In Mexico huitlacoche is a delicacy; the advanced source notes that the Hopi toast and eat it too, but **wawe' Iximulew man ntij ta**, here in Guatemala it is not eaten. Children paint their faces with its black dust at harvest, and its powder is dabbed on cuts as a remedy: **sokotajik** "wound" is itself a middle-voice noun, "what got injured".
- *Respect without theater.* Asking leave of the **Rajawal Juyu'** is a belief some families hold deeply, others lightly, others not at all. Describe it accurately (**nqak'utuj utzil chre**), follow your hosts' lead in the field, and never perform it as a party trick.

*Pitfalls for English speakers*

1. English "burned" hides three Kaqchikel sentences. Someone did it: **xuk'ät**. It was done (doer known or nameable): **xk'at**. It just happened: **xk'atitäj**. Choose on purpose.
2. No agent with the middle. "It got ruined by the rain" needs the passive or active (**ri jöb' xuyöj**, or **xyoj roma ri jöb'**), not *xyojtäj roma*.
3. The middle is intransitive: Set B only, and plural subjects show it: **xek'atitäj ri wäy**, not *xk'atitäj* when the tortillas are plural.
4. The linking vowel of **-täj** is learned per verb (**b'anatäj** but **k'atitäj** but **yojtäj**). Stick to attested forms; do not manufacture new ones freely.
5. **¿Achike xk'ulwachitäj?** asks about events; **¿Achike xaruk'ulwachij?** asks about *you*. Answering the first with "I'm fine" confuses; answer with what happened: **Majun, xa xpaxitäj jun läq.**
6. Growth stages are not interchangeable. Asking to buy **awän** at the market (you want **äj** or **ixim**) is like asking a US farmer to sell you "a corn". Use the stage you mean.

## Chapter 29: B'anob'äl - Crafts and the Work of Hands

- *How productive is -oy?* Treat it as a small, real pattern, not an open machine. The advanced source presents four compounds (kemoy po't, ponoy wäy, yuq'uy karne'l, b'anoy si'), the lexicalized q'atoy tzij, and the stacked ajb'anöy chakäch, ajb'onöy b'ojo'y. Read any new one you meet by the rule (antipassive n > y); to *produce* a maker-word beyond these, prefer -el, aj-, or the antipassive sentence.
- *Bare means bare.* In both nikemon po't and kemoy po't, the object never takes ri, taq, or a plural. If you need "the po't", you need the transitive verb back: nukem ri po't (Chapter 18's rule, now doing trade work).
- *rub'anik vs rub'anikil.* "How is it made?" ¿Achike rub'anik?; "what is it like?" ¿Achike rub'anikil? The advanced source's own headings also use rub'anoj for "the making"; same job.
- *Two q'or, two etz'ab'äl.* q'or "maize dough" vs q'or "lazy" (Chapter 9); etz'ab'äl "woven design, figure" vs etz'ab'äl "toy" (both current in the advanced source, and the small kites are called both things at once, which is rather the point).
- *Spelling variation as usual.* The advanced source writes kaq'ïq', chïk, wakamïn, rajïl with its systematic final lax vowels; this book keeps kaq'iq', chik, wakami, rajil (see Chapter 1). Its samajb'äl beside samajib'äl, and q'inab'äl beside q'inob'äl, are ordinary linking-vowel variation in -b'äl nouns (Chapter 8). Our -kem appears there as -këm.
- *Gender and craft.* Kaqchikel agent nouns are gender-neutral: an ajkem, a t'isonel, a b'anoy si' can be a woman, a man, or a non-binary person; only context tells you. In practice the crafts are gendered (backstrap-loom weaving is largely women's work; treadle looms were historically men's; mat-making is shared by design), but the boundaries are real only until they are crossed, and the advanced source's stories delight in crossing them, including a man whose basket falls apart because he thought "women's work" was easy.
- *A euphemism to know.* Chapter 25 noted it, and it matters in this chapter's domain: ajkem "weaver" is an old polite way to say a woman is pregnant. If someone smiles when you praise a bride as a weaver, that is why.
- *Pitfalls.* (1) English "she weaves po'ts" tempts you to *yerukem po't* with a plural object; the trade reading needs the antipassive, nikemon po't. (2) Do not build *-b'ej* instrumentals yourself; the voice is not productive. Say it with rik'in. (3) kemoy, ponoy end in y, not n; the n-forms are verbs, the y-forms are nouns.

## Chapter 30: Samaj - Work, Home, and Town

- *-xta- is a badge of two towns.* Produce it if your community does; otherwise say **chanin**. Comalapa and Poaquil speakers will understand your plain form, and you will understand their fast one. Do not extend **-xta-** to derived **-Vj** verbs; the attested pattern is on root verbs.
- *warab'äl jay: bedroom or hotel?* Our primary source, and Chapter 24, use **warab'äl jay** for "bedroom". The advanced source's town vocabulary glosses the same phrase "hotel" (a sleeping-house for travelers) and uses bare **warab'äl** for the bedroom. Both make sense ("sleeping place"); context decides, and in a town-center conversation the hotel reading is the likely one.
- *One clay word, two objects.* **Xot** is the tortilla griddle and the roof tile; **xot ruwi' jay** "roof xot" disambiguates. Likewise **xan** is both the adobe brick and the wall built of it, and by extension walls generally, even of block.
- *raqän jay.* Chapter 24 gave **raqän jay** "corridor" from our primary source. In the advanced source's building texts **raqän ri jay**, "the legs of the house", are its posts, alongside the more specific **ruxatatil jay**. Listen for which "leg" a speaker means.
- *pa che' "in jail".* Never "in the tree" in a town story. The phrase remembers the wooden stocks of colonial punishment.
- *Job words have no gender.* **Ajtz'aq**, **ch'ich'inel**, **q'atoy tzij**, **sokanel** apply to men and women alike; the advanced source's authors make a point of it. Add **ixöq** or **achin** only if the distinction matters: **jun ixöq ajtz'aq** "a woman mason".
- *A word to know and never use.* In the advanced source's street stories, learners meet **ixto / ixta**, a slur that some ladinos use for indigenous people; the story's whole point is the injustice of it. Recognize it, understand what has happened when you hear it, and do not repeat it.
- *Spelling drift.* The draft advanced source writes **wakamïn**, **ch'anin**, **chïk**, **k'a runaj chïk**; this book writes **wakami**, **chanin**, **chik**, **k'a runaj chik** (Chapter 10's one-word **k'arunaj** is the same expression). When you quote a text, keep its spelling; when you write your own, be consistent.
- *Money registers.* For large sums, most speakers switch to Spanish numbers (Chapter 10); the vigesimal forms (**wok'al manq'uq'** "a hundred quetzales", **lajk'al** "two hundred") are alive in careful speech and in bargaining.

*Pitfalls for English speakers*

1. Do not double the "quickly": **xinb'anxtaj** already contains it; *chanin xinb'anxtaj* is redundant (though speakers do it for emphasis).
2. **-(V)la'** replaces the **-j** of a derived verb; keep both and you get a non-word (*xuk'utujla'*). And the suffix needs a transitive host: "they walked and walked" is not built with **-la'**.
3. **K'as** is possessed by the ower, not the owed: **nuk'as awik'in** "my debt to you" (literally "my debt with you").
4. **-qäj** works both directions; **Xinqäj pwäq chre** is "I borrowed money from him" (money to-him being the source), so give the sentence a context or add **kan** ("lend out") when you mean lending.
5. **Rajïl** never stands bare: ask **¿Jampe rajïl?**, not *¿Jampe ajïl?*.
6. The migrant's money comes **pe** and goes **el** depending on who is speaking; get the directional from the speaker's position, not from English "send".

## Chapter 31: Yab'il chuqa' aq'om - Health and Healing

- *yawa' ixöq is not ixöq yawa'.* Adjective-first **yawa' ixöq** is the fixed, polite phrase for a PREGNANT woman; noun-first **ixöq yawa'** is simply a sick woman. The advanced source makes the contrast itself, asking students to explain **achike roma jun yawa' ixöq man junam ta rik'in jun ixöq yawa'** - why the two are not the same. Chapter 25's note on **yawa'** as a euphemism now has its grammar.
- *nq'axon and niq'axon.* The advanced source regularly writes the incompletive as **ni-** where this book, following our first source, writes **n-** before a zero 3sB (**niq'axon** vs **nq'axon**, **nitane'** vs **ntane'**). Same prefix, different spelling conventions; read both.
- *Quoting the advanced source.* Its lines above keep its own spellings: **ïn** for **in**, **wakamïn** for **wakami**, **chke** for **chike**, **po** "but". Data, not instructions (Chapter 26 discussed this).
- *Shivering.* **-b'ayb'öt** and **-b'erb'öt** are variants of the same trembling verb; the advanced source uses both. The chills idiom runs on **-silïl** "quiver": **nsilïl tew chwe** or **nsilïl tew chwij**.
- *Take care of yourself.* You will hear **tab'ana' kwenta awi'** with the Spanish loan **kwenta** (cuenta); the advanced source's doctor says it. The loan-free equivalent is **tachajij awi'**. Both are real usage; this book drills the second.
- *manta, once more.* When you read older or utz-awäch-style texts, **manta** + clause may be a POSITIVE counterfactual ("if I had money..."); in the advanced source's usage it is negative ("if ... had not"). Chapter 20's rule of thumb stands: try both readings, keep the one the sentence supports. In your own speech, **xa ta** (positive) and **xa manta** (negative) leave no doubt.
- *The pandemic's name.* **Q'eqaläj Jïq' Ojöb'**, "the terrible whooping cough", is the advanced source's coinage for COVID-19, shortened to **ri q'eqaläj ojöb'** on p. 231; **nimayab'il** "great illness" is the generic "pandemic". **q'eqaläj** is built on **q'ëq** "black, dark" with the **-aläj** intensifier of Chapter 9 - "black-awful".
- *iyom, k'exelom, ati't.* The midwife words form a couplet, **iyom k'exelom**, and a mother says **wiyom, nuk'exelom** of her own midwife. A third term, **ati't** "grandmother", is used too - but the possessed **wati't** for one's midwife belongs to the CHILD she delivered, who has in her a spiritual grandmother.

*Pitfalls for English speakers*

1. Do not translate "I have a fever" with a Set B pronoun: not *in k'atän* but **k'o k'atän chwij** - the fever is on you, not a property of you.
2. Do not make the sufferer the subject of **-q'axon**: "I hurt" is not *yiq'axon*; name the part: **nq'axon waqän** "my leg hurts".
3. **wi** cannot introduce a contrary-to-fact condition. "If I were a doctor" is **xa ta in aq'omanel**, never *wi in aq'omanel* (which would mean "if I am a doctor", a real possibility).
4. In a counterfactual, remember the **ta** in the RESULT clause: **Xa ta in ala', yib'iyin ta.** Dropping it leaves the result sounding factual.
5. "Not yet" in answers is **majani**, not *man ... ta*: **¿La xk'achoj? Majani.**
6. **ruloman ri jöb'** "during the rain" needs the noun with its article; bare *ruloman jöb'* sounds clipped.

## Chapter 32: Ri qach'ab'äl: Language, Community, and Nation

- *we ~ wi.* The conditional/disjunctive particle is **wi** in some towns, **we** in others, with no difference in meaning; the Kaqchikel Cholchi's own posts use **we**. This book has written **wi** since Chapter 23; produce whichever your community uses, and read both.
- *Names for the language.* Say **qach'ab'äl** among speakers, **Kaqchikel** or **Kaqchikel ch'ab'äl** when contrast is needed; Spanish is **kaxlan tzij**, or **kaxlan** alone once the topic is clear.
- *chi relatives are for your ears first.* In writing, prefer **ri** relatives, and keep the Chapter 18 antipassive rule when the head noun is the agent. Understand **chi** relatives everywhere; they are standard modern speech, not an error.
- *Purism is a register, not a law.* **Po**, **tons**, **i** are normal spoken Kaqchikel; **xa ja ri'**, **k'a ri'**, **chuqa'** are what a careful writer or radio announcer uses. Match your company, and never correct a speaker.
- *Feed spelling.* Expect missing apostrophes (**chuqa** for **chuqa'**), plain vowels for lax ones (**yojkikot**, **wakamin**), dialect **ruma / roma**, and Spanish or English mixed in. Restore the full forms silently when you read; use full ALMG spelling when you write.
- *Neologisms vary in uptake.* **Kematz'ib'**, **k'amaya'l** and **oyonib'äl** are in wide real use; others (like **let'et'**) live mostly in schools and print, while speakers say the Spanish word. Both facts are part of the sociolinguistic landscape; learn the coined word, and do not be surprised to hear *bicicleta*.
- *The advanced source's spellings.* The companion volume this chapter cites writes **wakamïn, rïn, chïk, chke** where this book writes **wakami, rin, chik, chike**, applying a word-final vowel-laxing rule more broadly. When you quote, keep the source's spelling; when you write, keep ours, consistently.
- *Respect vocabulary.* Words like **ajq'ij**, **Maya' Nimab'äl K'u'x** and **k'oxtum** name living religious practice. Use them as their users do, plainly and with respect; "brujo" and its English equivalents are slurs you will hear reported, never words to repeat.


# Dialect cheat sheet

Kaqchikel is spoken in several dozen municipalities across central Guatemala, which dialectologists group into regional varieties. This book follows the central varieties of Tecpán (Iximche') and Comalapa (Chiq'a'l), which also anchor the written standard. The table lists the differences a learner is most likely to hear or read. Abbreviations: CM Comalapa, TEC Tecpán, SO Sololá, LA Lake Atitlán towns, SAC San Antonio Aguas Calientes.

| Feature | This book | Variants and where |
|---|---|---|
| Lax vowels (ä ë ï ö ü) | all five, final syllables only | some varieties have fewer lax vowels or none: most towns today keep only ä, ë survives mainly in Poaquil, and each of ï, ö, ü is missing in many communities; when a suffix tenses the vowel (tab'ana', rub'anon) all dialects agree |
| "because of" | -oma (roma, woma) | -uma (ruma, wuma) is the majority form in the dialect survey, used in TEC itself, Patzicía, San Lucas Tolimán and most other towns; roma is recorded for Santo Domingo Xenacoj and San Marcos la Laguna (LA); both spellings circulate in print and teaching materials, and the conversational sources this book follows write roma, as does the same authors' newer the advanced source throughout |
| "with" | -ik'in (rik'in, wik'in) | -uk'in (ruk'in) in LA and older texts, and freely alongside rik'in in the authors' own newer prose |
| "now, today" | wakami | wakamïn (fuller form, the spelling the authors themselves now use), kami (south and west), wakamik, kamik (LA, under Tz'utujil and K'iche' influence) |
| 3s incompletive of short verbs | nel, nb'e, niwär | speech often inserts a dental stop: ndel, ntel, ndb'e; writing keeps n- |
| final m of possessed nouns | nutza'm, nupam, nutele'n | pronounced with n or ng in most towns (nutza'n, nupan); CM and TEC tend to ng, SAC to n; spelling keeps m when a suffix shows it |
| "go" prefix | b'e- (nb'esamäj) | CM often drops the b': nesamäj |
| rapid action | not marked (use aninäq, chanin) | CM and Poaquil add the suffix -xta- to an inflected verb, plus -n (intransitive) or -j (transitive): xelxtan "she left quickly", xkijaqxtaj "they opened it quickly"; less common elsewhere |
| "two" | ka'i' | ka'ib' kept by some speakers, especially daykeepers in ritual |
| passive of root transitives | vowel tensing (xb'an, xloq') | -Vx suffix (xchapäx, xtz'etëx) spreading, especially where lax vowels are few |
| "where" | akuchi' | ak'uchi, k'uchi, k'uchi'; ape' |
| "what" | achike | tux, atux, antux; nak (LA) |
| "rain" | jöb' | jäb' |
| "dog" | tz'i' | unpossessed tz'e' in most towns; tz'i' when possessed |
| "cat" | mes | mis, syan, lu'x |
| "sheep" | karne'l | chij |
| "chayote" | k'ix | ch'ima' / ch'uma' (TEC, San Marcos la Laguna, San Lucas Tolimán). **Warning:** in most other varieties, ch'ima' said to an adult means "vagina"; outside those towns, say k'ix |
| "salt" | atz'am | atz'an |
| "potato" | is | saqwäch, paps |
| "I" | rin | yin, ri'in, in re' |
| "we" | röj | roj, ri'oj |
| "you (pl)" | rix | ri'ix |
| "no" | manäq | näq; mani (often ni in children's speech) |
| title for a man | ma (adult), a (young) | ma marks respect in most towns, but in San Pedro Sacatepéquez and SAC it is felt as disrespectful; there a is the safe choice (San Pedro Sacatepéquez says ri'j a Xwan for an elderly don Juan), and Santa María Cauqué generalizes a to boys, young men and grown men alike |
| title for a woman | te (adult), xta (young) | ya competing with te in some towns; elsewhere ya for older women; titles falling out of use in places |
| "twenty" | juk'al (things), juwinäq (people, time) | winäq generalizing to all counting |
| eighty | kajk'al | jumuch' (muchi' units), kajwinäq |
| "then" | k'a ri' | k'a ri, k'ari; Spanish tons in speech |
| plural of mouse, star | taq ch'oy, taq ch'umil | ch'oyi', ch'umila' for speakers who treat them as animate; Maxwell's newer grammar makes the star case contextual: taq ch'umil for stars as distant objects, ch'umila' when they act on our lives |
| "see you later" | ch'o'n chik k'a | ch'o'n yan chik |
